title: The Lamborghini Cheetah Is the Forgotten Prototype That Spawned the LM002

body_markdown:
Launched in 1986,[the Lamborghini LM002](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/the-lamborghini-lm002-makes-a-strong-case-for-the-impractical-classic/) seemingly came out of nowhere. It was built by a brand with no off-roading heritage, and it looked nothing like the poster-worthy supercars that it shared showroom space with. And yet, its existence wasn’t as random as it might seem. The LM002 evolved from a prototype called Cheetah that Lamborghini tried to sell to the United States military.


The project started in the late 1970s, which was not a glittering time for Lamborghini. The company was hit hard by the 1973 oil crisis, and Ferruccio Lamborghini[gradually sold his shares](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/lamborghinis-wild-ownership-history-is-almost-as-colorful-as-its-cars/) in the company he founded to Swiss investors. The brand found itself in dire financial straits and began looking for ways to stay afloat. It inked a deal with BMW to design a race car powered by a mid-mounted engine, which later became[the M1](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/history-of-the-bmw-m1/) , and it hoped that a lucrative contract with the United States military would give it much-needed cash. At the time, the Army was looking for a new all-terrain vehicle to replace its aging fleet of light off-roaders.


Mobility Technology International (MTI) worked with Lamborghini on the project, and the Cheetah made its debut in 1977. It certainly looked ready for combat with huge tires, a generous amount of ground clearance, and flat fiberglass body panels. It featured a tubular roll cage; its front end was fitted with a massive skid plate, and it had neither doors nor a roof. It’s not difficult to imagine Cheetah offshoots with doors, a roof, or a wagon-like body, however. Army officials needed a versatile vehicle, after all.

Regardless of the angle from which you approach it, the Cheetah could pass as[a Meyers Manx](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/classic-meyers-manx-dune-buggy-reborn-with-new-diy-kit/) that went through a Pokemon-style evolution. The similar proportions aren’t a coincidence. Like the Manx, the Cheetah is powered by a rear-mounted engine. But instead of a Volkswagen-sourced air-cooled flat-four, it’s fitted with a 5.9-liter V-8 borrowed from the Chrysler parts bin and linked to a three-speed automatic transmission. The engine sent about 183 horsepower to the four wheels via a two-speed transfer case.


The limitations of a 180-horsepower engine in a 4500-pound car quickly became clear during testing, and Lamborghini’s archives department notes that engineers later experimented with a more powerful engine. However, no amount of power could overcome what many considered to be the Cheetah’s main drawback: Its rear-heavy weight distribution. There was so much weight over the rear axle that the Cheetah reportedly earned a reputation for unpredictable handling and dangerously haphazard steering.


Legal problems also permeated the project. MTI was founded by former FMC employees, and the Cheetah turned out to be influenced by an earlier military prototype called FMC XR311. FMC sued both Lamborghini and MTI shortly after the Cheetah made its debut. The outcome of the lawsuit is lost to history, but the cost of developing an unsuccessful prototype and defending it in court broke Lamborghini financially. BMW feared the worst as it watched from the sidelines, and it canceled its contract with Lamborghini to develop the M1. Lamborghini filed for bankruptcy in 1978 and was managed by the Italian government until 1980.

Some sources claim that Lamborghini built a single example of the Cheetah and that it was destroyed during testing, but that’s not accurate. Two examples were built, according to Lamborghini, and only one remains. It’s owned by a private collector, though it’s occasionally loaned out to Lamborghini for events. While the Cheetah project was quickly scrapped, it had a lasting influence on Lamborghini as the brand entered the 1980s. The company built a second off-roading prototype called LM001 and presented it at the 1981 Geneva auto show. It featured numerous updates over the Cheetah, including a closed body, but it remained rear-engined.


Slowly but surely, Lamborghini’s idea of the perfect SUV was taking shape. The company built a third prototype called LMA002 that made its debut in 1982 with a Countach-sourced, 4.8-liter V-12 mounted in the front. This one-off spawned the LM002, which entered production in 1986 with the Countach Quattrovalvole’s 450-horsepower, 5.2-liter V-12 between its squared-off fenders.


In the meantime, AM General had secured the United States Army contract that Lamborghini was after with[the Humvee](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/2023-bull-market-pick-1992-06-am-general-hummer-h1/) .
